problem: Classical task planners (PDDL/Fast Downward) assume full knowledge of object locations and cannot plan when task-critical objects are missing. Learned object-search methods are standalone modules and cannot be integrated into a task planner that must decide what to look for and when.
motivation: Mobile robots in homes always face missing objects, so they must search. Search actions are stochastic, and planning over them is expensive and incompatible with deterministic solvers. The paper packages a search policy inside a deterministic high-level action whose cost is the policy's expected cost, so existing solvers can be reused.
key_idea: Define a deterministic high-level PDDL find(obj, start, target) action, instantiated by a learning-informed model-based object search policy (LIOS) whose Bellman expected cost is used as the action cost in planning.
insight: Both parts matter. Using LIOS for search alone (OptLIOS/PesLIOS) beats Greedy search in every scenario. Replacing naive optimistic/pessimistic find costs with the model-based expected cost gives further gains, e.g. Deliver 3-Object 94.58 vs 108.62 and Any-of-Three 22.03 vs 22.72. Accurate expected costs let the planner choose which object to seek and in what order, which fixed heuristic costs cannot do.
method: find action: deterministic PDDL action (start, search until found, pick up, move to target) that hides search stochasticity; object state variables are treated optimistically and repaired by replanning
LIOS policy: a learned per-container probability of finding the object, combined with model-based planning over the order of container searches to minimize expected cost

Expected cost: a Bellman equation Q^pi_o combining move+search cost, the found branch (pick + move to target) and the not-found branch (recursion over remaining containers); this becomes find-cost in PDDL
Probability estimator: Sentence-BERT embeddings of room, container and object names plus one-hot vectors feed a fully connected network trained with cross-entropy on data from 500 ProcTHOR maps

Planning loop: Fast Downward (FF-astar2) plans with find actions; LIOS policies are recomputed only when a find is selected, use at most 8 unsearched containers, and the robot replans after every observation

setting.backbone: Sentence-BERT encoder + fully connected MLP for object-location probabilities; Fast Downward PDDL planner with model-based search policy
setting.training_data: Supervised labels of object-in-container occurrences from 500 ProcTHOR maps
setting.observation: Known map layout and container locations, with the contents of searched containers revealed (symbolic); Spot uses LiDAR mapping and AR-marker object detection
setting.action_space: High-level symbolic PDDL actions (find, pick, place, move, make-coffee, etc.) with A*/move_base navigation
setting.privileged: Known map with searchable containers and the set of objects that exist; no GT object locations

numbers.evidence: "Our LIOS strategy results in an improvement of 59.9% compared to the simple Greedy baseline over the 200 object search trials."

numbers_note: Real-world Spot results are reported mainly in a figure; the text gives config A times: ModelLIOS 174s vs PesLIOS 264s vs PesGreedy 311s. Success rates are given as percentages.
results: ModelLIOS achieves the lowest average cost in all five ProcTHOR scenarios (e.g. Deliver 3-Object 94.58 vs the best baseline OptLIOS at 108.62). Success rates are competitive, but lower on Breakfast+Coffee (83%, versus 90% for OptGreedy). LIOS search improves cost by 59.9% over Greedy in isolation. On Spot, ModelLIOS is best in configuration A (174s vs 264s and 311s) but slightly worse in B and D.
limitations: find searches for one object at a time, with no concurrent or opportunistic search while navigating
Object state (e.g. clean/dirty) is treated optimistically and repaired by replanning
Assumes a known map with searchable containers and a known set of existing objects; the real-world evaluation is small (4 configurations)
builds_on: Stein et al. 2018 (learning-informed planning for point-goal navigation in unknown environments)
